docs.title: State Storage
docs.text:
• States stored as foreign key references to reference data tables (not C# enums)
  • Allows runtime configuration of valid states
  • Enables future workflow customization per division/office
  • Transition validation logic typically in domain service layer
  • State change events published to message queue for integrations

docs.title: Validation Enforcement Points
docs.text:
• Pre-save validation: Catch violations before database insert
  • Pre-transition validation: Enforce state machine rules during status updates
  • Post-save events: Publish domain events (Activity.StateChanged) for async workflows
  • Query-time filtering: Soft-deleted, expired, and archived records excluded by default

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• Unit tests for each valid state transition
  • Unit tests for each invalid transition attempt
  • Integration tests for cross-entity validations (e.g., Contact + Activity + Tenancy workflow)
  • Use Gherkin scenarios as acceptance criteria for complex business rules

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This directory documents the existing Hub user interface as a product and interaction specification. It intentionally describes screens, navigation, user actions, validation, feedback, and API-facing behavior without making Angular a requirement for a replacement implementation.

The documentation is based on the source at:

C:\Source\Devops\KnightFrank.hub\src\KnightFrank.Antares.Angular

It records implemented behavior, not necessarily approved future business behavior. The product and subject-matter review items in traceability and open questions remain important.

docs.title: Document set
docs.text: Document Contents Parity specification Rules for producing a faithful replacement from the vault Layout and sizing Measured shell dimensions and layout conventions Page specifications Page-by-page parity inventory and coverage Navigation and access Application shell, navigation, recent-item drawers, routes, and role visibility Screen catalogue Screen families and the responsibilities of each domain area User interactions and workflows Search, edit, state changes, documents, matching, communications, and dashboard behavior Shared UI and feedback Reusable controls, layout conventions, loading, errors, notifications, and responsive behavior API interaction contract UI-to-service interaction patterns and the data needed by replacement screens Traceability and open questions Source evidence, confidence levels, and items requiring product or UX confirmation

docs.title: Replacement implementation principle
docs.text:
A replacement should preserve:

  • the user-visible route and screen responsibilities;
  • the search, preview, detail, edit, and relationship-panel flows;
  • role-based visibility and authorization outcomes;
  • client-side validation and calculated values;
  • server-backed validation before important state transitions;
  • confirmation, error, loading, and refresh behavior;
  • the relationships between contacts, companies, properties, activities, requirements, offers, tenancies, documents, and communications.

The replacement does not need to preserve Angular modules, generated client classes, RxJS services, Angular Material, or the current folder structure.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: This specification defines the as-is Hub GUI that a replacement application must reproduce. It is not a redesign brief. Angular is only the source implementation; the target specification is the observable page, layout, field, validation, interaction, and feedback behavior.

docs.title: Fidelity levels
docs.text:
Level Meaning P0 Route/page exists and has the same user responsibility P1 Tabs, panels, dialogs, commands, and navigation match P2 Fields, labels, control types, defaults, visibility, and validation match P3 Layout dimensions, spacing, responsive behavior, styling, and feedback match P4 Rendered output is verified against the existing GUI at representative viewport/data states

The current vault is at P0-P1 for most areas and P2 for selected core workflows. The new page specifications are intended to move the project toward P2-P3 before any replacement implementation is generated.

docs.title: Canonical page specification
docs.text:
Each page document should describe:

  1. route and entry points;
  2. page title and environment context;
  3. page regions, columns, tabs, accordions, and panels;
  4. fields and controls;
  5. initial data and lookup requests;
  6. defaults and conditional visibility;
  7. client-side validation;
  8. server-side validation and commands;
  9. loading, empty, warning, error, and success states;
  10. dirty-form and navigation behavior;
  11. refresh and route-reuse behavior;
  12. role restrictions;
  13. responsive and sizing rules;
  14. source evidence.

docs.title: Source-of-truth hierarchy
docs.text:
When evidence conflicts, use this order:

  1. rendered behavior verified in the existing application;
  2. page template and style source;
  3. page component and resolver logic;
  4. shared control implementation;
  5. generated API client and API/domain documentation;
  6. existing vault summaries.

The vault should record the result and retain the source path for traceability.

docs.title: What can be generated from the parity specification
docs.text:
A replacement framework can be generated once the page documents contain:

  • route and page metadata;
  • a field/control schema;
  • a validation schema;
  • a layout schema;
  • an interaction/state schema;
  • API operation mappings;
  • visual tokens and screenshot references where pixel parity is required.

The replacement should not reproduce Angular module boundaries, generated client class names, or RxJS implementation details unless they are needed for compatibility.

docs.title: API interaction contract
docs.text: This document records what replacement screens need from the server. It is not an OpenAPI specification; the generated client remains the detailed method-level endpoint inventory.

docs.title: Request model
docs.text:
The UI constructs requests from:

  • route parameters and parent entity identifiers;
  • search criteria, filters, sort, paging, selected columns, and map bounds;
  • reactive form values and selected lookup records;
  • current user and, where applicable, proxy-user context;
  • runtime configuration such as the API root and localization settings.

The effective REST shape is generally:

{runtime rootUrl}/api/{resource}/{operation}[/{id}][/{sub-resource}]

docs.title: Operation families
docs.text: Operation Typical use GET /{resource}/{id} Load a detail or profile GET /{resource}/{id}/preview Load a lightweight preview GET /{resource}/{id}/editData Load edit data and lookup context POST /{resource}/search Execute a paged search POST /{resource} Create a record or command PUT /{resource}/{id} Update a record DELETE /{resource}/{id} Delete or remove a record/association POST /{resource}/{id}/activities Query or create related activities POST /{resource}/{id}/notes Create or query related notes POST /{resource}/{id}/attachments Upload or attach documents DELETE /{resource}/{id}/attachments/{attachmentId} Remove an attachment POST /{resource}/{id}/stateValidate Validate a candidate state transition PUT /{resource}/{id}/parties Update people or party relationships PUT /{resource}/{id}/addresses Update addresses POST /activities/matches/{id} Manage activity/requirement matching POST /activities/{id}/termsAndConditions Manage activity terms POST /viewings Create or update a viewing PUT /viewingtours Update a viewing tour POST /widgets/{area} Load dashboard widget data POST /widgets/{area}/drilldown Load widget drill-down data GET /attachments and related operations List and manage documents GET /wopi/files/{fileId} Online document content interaction GET /watermarks/{entityId} Image/document processing support

docs.title: Service groupings
docs.text:
Replacement screens need equivalent server capabilities for:

  • activities, appointments, offers, and requirements;
  • contacts, consent, and callback lists;
  • companies, businesses, ownership, and property hierarchy;
  • properties, buildings, developments, estates, phases, and portfolios;
  • tenancies, progression, renewal, termination, paperwork, and Qube;
  • attachments, document templates, WOPI, watermarks, and portal visibility;
  • emails, text messages, notifications, notes, and external messages;
  • dashboards, widgets, saved searches, latest views, and preferences;
  • users, departments, configuration, translations, subscriptions, and Dotmailer;
  • reports, publication events, Thirdfort, web enquiries, and other integrations.

docs.title: Response behavior required by the UI
docs.text:
Responses need to communicate more than a record payload:

  • typed detail, preview, search-result, and edit-data models;
  • paging totals and result rows;
  • lookup and enum values;
  • validation failures and status-specific required fields;
  • authorization failures;
  • command success/failure and user-readable messages;
  • updated identifiers and refresh requirements;
  • attachment upload progress and metadata;
  • notification, publication, and integration outcomes where relevant.

docs.title: Authority boundaries
docs.text:
The client owns presentation behavior and immediate form validation. The server remains authoritative for:

  • authorization;
  • entity existence and concurrency;
  • state-transition validity;
  • cross-entity business rules;
  • persistence;
  • integration outcomes;
  • document permissions and visibility.

The replacement must preserve these boundaries even if its client technology changes.

The source repeatedly uses these layout classes and patterns:

docs.title: Responsive behavior
docs.text:
The source explicitly changes the main menu at small and extra-small breakpoints. Page templates also use responsive Bootstrap-style columns, but screen-by-screen behavior depends on the rendered CSS and content. A full replacement must verify:

  • column collapse order;
  • minimum field widths;
  • horizontal table overflow;
  • sticky footer behavior;
  • modal and side-panel width;
  • map and gallery behavior;
  • keyboard and touch targets.

docs.title: Application shell
docs.text:
Authenticated screens use a shared shell:

  1. A left main menu provides domain navigation.
  2. The top bar shows the environment name and current page title.
  3. The top bar exposes unread notifications, help/what's-new links, and proxy user login.
  4. The content area displays the active screen.
  5. Unknown routes are redirected; unauthorised routes are sent to the not-found outcome.

At startup the shell loads general configuration, latest views, country data, locales, markets and sectors, and telephone formatting data before entering the child screen.

The menu starts minimized. A domain menu item can expand to show sub-items. Selecting another item collapses the previous item. Small and extra-small breakpoints switch the menu into mobile mode. Domain menus can also show a recent-items drawer.

docs.title: Screen catalogue
docs.text: This catalogue describes the visible responsibilities of the GUI. A screen may be composed of a route, tabs, panels, dialogs, grids, and related-record components rather than a single page.

docs.title: Common screen families
docs.text: Family User experience Search/list Enter criteria, run a paged query, inspect a grid/table, open a preview or detail view Add/create Select a creation context, enter a form, validate, save, and continue to the new record Edit Load existing data and lookups, change fields, validate, save, and refresh the record View/profile Show summary and detail information, then navigate related tabs and panels Relationship panel Query children using the parent identifier and create or update associations Preview panel Show a lightweight record view without leaving the current list or parent page Modal/dialog Complete a focused command such as confirmation, upload, selection, merge, or validation Publication/marketing Manage publication state, images, brochures, visibility, and marketing actions Administration Work with role-protected configuration lists and edit dialogs

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: The dashboard is a configurable work surface. It contains widgets for activities, requirements, tenancies, callbacks, CDD, marketing, instructions, web enquiries, property visits, notifications, business generation, market overview, and other operational areas. Widgets provide counters, lists, calendar views, and drill-down actions. SignalR-backed notifications can update the notification state.

docs.title: Contacts
docs.text: Contact screens support search, create, edit, and profile views. A contact profile brings together personal details, addresses, phones and emails, activities, requirements, referrals, interests, negotiators, consent, notes, communications, and related companies.

docs.title: Companies
docs.text: Company screens support search, create, edit, and profile views. Company profiles expose contacts, activities, requirements, instructions, ownership, tenancies, interests, addresses, notes, and related property information.

docs.title: Properties and property hierarchy
docs.text:
Property screens cover search, create/edit, property checks, profile views, ownership, activities, attachments, publication, marketing, and related assets. Development, building, estate, phase, and portfolio areas provide hierarchical or grouped property views:

  • developments contain buildings and units;
  • buildings expose units, ownership, activities, attachments, and property breakdown;
  • estates and phases expose related property and activity management;
  • portfolios coordinate properties and tenancies at portfolio level.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text: Activity screens cover search, create/edit, preview, parties, terms and conditions, publication, marketing assets, offers, requirements, matches, viewings, appointments, referrals, and state changes. The edit experience varies by service line and creation context, including activity creation from properties, buildings, developments, estates, phases, portfolios, and other records.

docs.title: Requirements and matching
docs.text: Requirement screens support search, saved searches, create/edit, applicant management, matching, viewing tours, progression, and instruction linkage. Matching screens connect requirements to activities and allow users to progress or arrange viewings.

docs.title: Offers
docs.text: Offer screens support search, create/edit, preview, acceptance, rejection, withdrawal, reservation-specific status handling, and linkage to an activity. Offer forms calculate and validate price, area-based amounts, annual amounts, and lease dates where applicable.

docs.title: Tenancies
docs.text: Tenancy screens support search, view/edit, progression, renewal, termination, deposit protection, paperwork upload, email upload, appointments, compliance, and related parties. Tenancy workflows can be initiated from properties, estates, activities, and other contexts.

docs.title: Instructions, pitches, and referrals
docs.text: These areas provide search, create/edit, view, related activity, task, document, and progression behavior. Referral and instruction creation can be entered from related requirements, activities, or referrals.

docs.title: Marketing lists
docs.text: Marketing-list screens support search, create/edit, contact upload, contact editing, merge, export, and related marketing communication behavior. Merge is restricted to the Marketeer role.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: The report area lets the user select a report, provide criteria, generate the result, and download or view the output. Domain menus can open this area with a preselected report group.

docs.title: Administration and configuration
docs.text: Administration provides tabs and dialogs for users, departments, Dotmailer, configurations, templates, showovers, marketing communication topics, subscriptions, LIA rules, and portal document visibility. Configuration provides system configuration and translations and is limited to system administrators.

docs.title: Shared content available across domains
docs.text:
Most major records can expose:

  • activities and current activities;
  • notes and journal/history;
  • attachments and document previews;
  • addresses, contacts, ownership, and parties;
  • appointments, viewings, emails, text messages, and notifications;
  • maps and location information;
  • status, alerts, consent, CDD, and compliance information;
  • related-record search and navigation.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: The catalogue is based on the feature folders under src/app/, the route modules, component templates, and the existing Angular GUI analysis.

docs.title: Layout vocabulary
docs.text:
The GUI uses a consistent vocabulary of reusable interaction surfaces:

  • page-level search and edit screens;
  • cards and information boxes for summaries;
  • tabs and collapsible sections for dense records;
  • side panels and preview panels for related or lightweight views;
  • modal dialogs for focused commands and confirmation;
  • grids and paginators for result sets;
  • context menus and action buttons for record commands;
  • toast notifications for command outcomes;
  • busy containers and progress indicators during loading;
  • attachment pickers and file-drop upload areas;
  • map and address controls for location data.

The replacement should preserve the information hierarchy and task sequence, not necessarily the current component names.

docs.title: Reusable controls
docs.text:
Source feature areas show reusable controls for:

  • addresses, maps, phone numbers, emails, dates, date ranges, numbers, prices, rich text, checkboxes, radio buttons, toggles, and enum selections;
  • typeahead and searchable resource selectors;
  • users, departments, companies, contacts, properties, requirements, and activities;
  • notes, alerts, consent, CDD validity, ownership, fee splits, invoices, and lease details;
  • attachments, document previews, WOPI, generated documents, watermarks, and portal visibility;
  • appointments, attendees, viewing tours, emails, text messages, and notifications;
  • search results tables, maps, pagination, columns, sorting, and export.

docs.title: Form conventions
docs.text:
The implemented forms use the following observable conventions:

  • fields use a filled appearance with labels that remain visible;
  • required markers are hidden in favor of validation behavior;
  • form-field supporting text sizes dynamically;
  • pagination hides the page-size selector by default;
  • select controls use delayed typeahead filtering;
  • tabs are not stretched to fill the whole width;
  • destructive or irreversible commands generally require confirmation;
  • field validation includes required fields, maximum lengths, non-negative amounts, positive minimum rents, and date-range rules where relevant.

docs.title: Loading and empty states
docs.text:
Screens load configuration and related data before rendering when the data is required to form the page. During asynchronous work the UI uses busy containers, progress indicators, or disabled command states. Search and relationship panels must distinguish:

  • not yet searched;
  • loading;
  • successful search with zero results;
  • successful search with results;
  • failed request.

This distinction is important for a replacement because an empty result is not the same as an unavailable service.

docs.title: Unsaved changes and navigation
docs.text:
Unsaved-change protection is implemented, but it is not a global rule for every form:

  • selected edit and administration routes use a navigation-block guard;
  • a blocked route opens a confirmation modal before navigation;
  • browser-level navigation also registers a beforeunload handler;
  • confirming the discard unblocks navigation and clears the browser handler;
  • the quick-create, activity add/edit/view, instruction, and selected administration flows are among the routes using this behavior;
  • other forms must be checked individually rather than assumed to have the same protection.

The replacement should make the scope of draft protection explicit and should not silently lose edits when a user changes route, closes a panel, or leaves the browser.

docs.title: Errors and notifications
docs.text:
Shared HTTP behavior handles XSS-related processing, API errors, date conversion, and proxy-user context. API errors are surfaced through common feedback rather than silently converted into successful results.

The current global HTTP outcomes are:

Response Current GUI outcome 400 GET responses may show formatted API errors; some legacy branches remain migration TODOs 401 The interceptor contains a migration TODO; a definitive current redirect is not evidenced here 403 Navigate to the no-access screen 404 Navigate to the not-found screen 405 The interceptor contains a migration TODO 408 Show the shared HTTP response error 503 Reload the application to display the offline state 500-599 Show the shared HTTP response error

Successful responses can also carry X-ErrorMessages and X-WarningMessages headers, which are queued for shared display. This means the replacement API contract must support both HTTP failures and successful responses containing user-visible warnings.

Toasts are positioned at the top center, prevent duplicates, include a close button, and remain available long enough for the user to read them. The top-bar bell distinguishes unread and read notification states and displays an unread count.

docs.title: Responsive and browser behavior
docs.text:
The main menu observes small and extra-small breakpoints and switches to mobile mode. The shell also displays a browser compatibility message when the current browser is not Chrome. Detailed responsive breakpoints, field ordering, and screen-specific layout behavior still require visual review of the templates and styles.

Responsive behavior is therefore confirmed for the shell navigation, but not yet specified as a complete responsive contract for every domain screen.

docs.title: Route reuse and refresh behavior
docs.text:
The current GUI does not always recreate a screen when navigation changes. A custom route-reuse policy can preserve the current component or reset it based on:

  • the route's reset mode;
  • empty query parameters;
  • any route-parameter change.

Replacement screens should define when filters, selected tabs, scroll position, and unsaved form state are retained versus reloaded.

docs.title: Accessibility evidence and limits
docs.text: The source includes accessible behavior in places, including hidden decorative icons, material labels, close-button labels, and keyboard-oriented controls such as autocomplete. However, the source review does not establish complete keyboard traversal, focus order, screen-reader announcements, contrast, touch-target, or error-announcement compliance for the whole application. Accessibility remains a validation activity, not a resolved behavior.

docs.title: Localization and configuration
docs.text: Labels and messages are translation-key based. Runtime configuration supplies the API root and other application settings. A replacement should separate display text, runtime configuration, and business data so that translations and environment-specific settings remain changeable.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: The shared behavior is evidenced by src/app/app.module.ts, src/app/layout/, src/app/common/, shared component templates and styles, and the existing Angular GUI analysis.

docs.title: High confidence
docs.text:
• Route names and route-level role guards.
  • Main-menu entries and role filtering.
  • Existence of search, create, edit, view, preview, panel, and modal screen patterns.
  • API service and endpoint families in generated client code.
  • Shared shell, interceptor, notification, and configuration behavior.

docs.title: Medium confidence
docs.text:
• Exact screen labels and field ordering.
  • Which related panels appear for every record subtype.
  • Which widget configurations are enabled in each environment.
  • Whether a generated API service is used by a visible screen, an integration, an administration feature, or a future screen.

docs.title: Requires product or SME confirmation
docs.text:
• Whether source-derived client behavior is approved business policy.
  • Status vocabulary and transition meaning where client and server enums may drift.
  • Required fields and workflow steps for every service line and market.
  • The intended user experience for errors, empty states, and exceptional paths.

docs.title: Source review findings
docs.text:
The following questions have been progressed from open questions to source-confirmed behavior:

Question Source finding Status How is navigation protected when edits are incomplete? Selected edit and administration routes use a navigation-block guard and confirmation modal; browser unload is also blocked while the service is active. Confirmed, partial route coverage How are common HTTP failures handled? 403 navigates to noAccess, 404 to notFound, 408 and 5xx show a shared HTTP error, and 503 reloads the application. Some 400, 401, and 405 paths retain migration TODOs. Confirmed, with incomplete legacy paths What responsive behavior exists? The main menu observes small and extra-small breakpoints and switches to mobile mode. Confirmed for shell; screen-level behavior open What loading behavior exists? Busy containers, page spinners, labels, and component-level busy flags are used for asynchronous work. Confirmed; exact empty-state copy varies by screen Is route state retained? A custom route-reuse strategy can preserve or reset a component based on route config, reset mode, query parameters, or route parameter changes. Confirmed Is accessibility complete? The source contains some ARIA labels/hidden decorative icons and labelled controls, but no whole-application accessibility evidence. Partial; audit required

These findings are implementation facts. They do not by themselves establish that the behavior is the desired future product behavior.

docs.title: Open UX questions
docs.text:
1. Which screens and panels are used most frequently by each user role?
  2. Which layouts, columns, tabs, and fields are mandatory versus configurable?
  3. What responsive behavior is required beyond the current mobile menu mode?
  4. Which browser support is required now that the current GUI favors Chrome?
  5. Which keyboard, accessibility, and screen-reader behaviors are required?
  6. Which visual assets, branding, icons, and report previews must be retained?
  7. Which workflows need unsaved-change warnings or draft recovery?
  8. Which long-running operations need progress, cancellation, or resumability?

docs.title: Questions narrowed by source review
docs.text:
• The current mobile requirement is limited to a responsive navigation mode; screen-level responsive requirements still need a decision.
  • Draft protection exists on selected routes, but the complete list of routes that must protect unsaved work needs product confirmation.
  • Browser support is currently signaled toward Chrome, but the supported replacement browser matrix is undecided.
  • Accessibility cannot be inferred as complete from the existing ARIA usage; a target standard and test scope are still needed.

docs.title: Open behavioral questions
docs.text:
1. Which client-side defaults and calculations are contractual?
  2. Which status transitions require a hard confirmation step?
  3. What are the exact refresh and event rules after each command?
  4. Which attachment visibility and document actions are role restricted?
  5. What are the concurrency and stale-data rules when two users edit a record?
  6. What should the user see when an asynchronous integration is pending or fails?

docs.title: Behaviors now evidenced by source
docs.text:
• State-change validation is a server call followed by conditional panels, confirmation, command submission, and refresh.
  • HTTP authorization and not-found failures have distinct navigation outcomes.
  • General server warnings and error headers are queued for shared display.
  • Long-running actions can use a labelled page spinner or busy container, but cancellation and resumability are not established as general behavior.
  • Route reuse can preserve a screen or force a reset when route parameters or query state changes.

docs.title: Documentation limits
docs.text:
This set documents the GUI as observed in source. It does not replace:

  • a visual walkthrough with representative users;
  • a complete design-system inventory;
  • an OpenAPI contract;
  • accessibility testing;
  • browser/device testing;
  • product acceptance criteria;
  • production configuration and operational runbooks.

The existing Planning README records the outstanding SME and detailed UX review work.

docs.title: Search to detail
docs.text:
1. The user opens a domain search screen.
  2. Lookup data and configuration are loaded.
  3. The user enters criteria and runs the search.
  4. The UI displays paged results, with optional map, column, sort, and filter controls.
  5. The user opens a preview panel or navigates to the full record.
  6. The detail view loads related panels and allows further commands.

Search screens commonly support saved searches, export, subscriptions, bulk actions, recent records, and navigation between result records.

docs.title: Create and edit
docs.text:
1. The user chooses a create action or enters an edit route.
  2. The UI loads edit data, lookups, configuration, enums, and related context.
  3. The form is populated, including defaults derived from the selected context.
  4. Field-level and cross-field validation runs while the user edits.
  5. The user confirms the command where the action is consequential.
  6. The UI submits create or update data.
  7. Success is shown with a toast or navigation; the parent and related panels are refreshed.
  8. API errors remain visible through shared error handling.

docs.title: Status changes
docs.text:
Status changes are not treated as a simple dropdown update:

  1. The user selects a candidate status.
  2. The UI calls server-side validation, such as POST /api/activities/{id}/stateValidate or POST /api/requirements/{id}/stateValidate.
  3. The response determines required information and panels, such as notes, completion dates, exchanged dates, lost-to information, negotiator restrictions, CDD, rent data, or marketing requirements.
  4. The user completes the required information and confirms the action.
  5. The UI submits the state/update command.
  6. The record, activity feed, related panels, and relevant projections are refreshed.

The API is authoritative for business transition validity. A replacement must not rely on client validation alone.

docs.title: Activity and offer behavior
docs.text:
The GUI contains behavior that must be preserved independently of its framework:

  • instructed and marketed dates can be defaulted for configured activity statuses;
  • status controls change visible fields based on the selected status;
  • referral and publication controls depend on activity status;
  • completion ownership choices depend on completion/letting status, agency, service line, accepted offers, applicant/requirement presence, and ownership type;
  • offer status choices vary by offer type;
  • reservation offers are restricted to reserved and withdrawn outcomes;
  • accepted offers can default agreed price from offer price;
  • area-based and annual amounts are converted for display and submission;
  • lease dates are calculated from week/month periods and rejected when invalid, expired, inverted, or beyond the remaining lease duration.

These behaviors are implementation evidence and should be confirmed by an SME before being treated as new product policy.

docs.title: Related records and panels
docs.text:
Parent screens load child records by parent ID. Common actions include:

  • add or edit an activity from a property, contact, company, or requirement;
  • add requirements and activities to a contact or company;
  • connect offers and matches to activities;
  • manage ownership and parties;
  • create viewing tours from matched activities;
  • add notes, appointments, emails, text messages, and referrals;

docs.title: Feedback and refresh expectations
docs.text:

  • refreshes the edited record;

  • updates the current list or navigates to the next screen;
  • publishes or reacts to relevant notification/publication events.

After an error, the UI keeps the user in context and surfaces the API error through shared error handling rather than treating the command as successful.
